Delhi
Camp break. Thirty-six hours. You land in Delhi with a backpack and no plan. The air tastes like smoke and winter.
You came. I said "if you're ever in Delhi". People don't usually take that literally.
Two years. She cut her hair. She still holds the red pen like it's a weapon.
Two years of video calls and you're finally here. Your face is smaller in real life.
She hugs you for a long time. Long enough that the chai seller on the corner looks away politely.
I'm here as a reporter. You're here as a story. Sit.
I deserved that.
Listen. I've been on Mehra Sports Group for eight months. Shell companies inside shell companies.
Sunny's court papers mention a "Mr. M" thirty-seven times. And there's another name next to Mehra's that I can't explain.
Karan Dhillon. Payments from the captain to a Mehra company. Forty crore in two years.
Your captain is either corrupt, or somebody is bleeding him dry. You're in that camp. Which is it?
Tell her about the tunnel.
She'll know what to do with it.
"I can't tell you. Not yet."
Protect Karan.
"Not yet." So there is something. Fine. I'll find it without you. I always do.
"Keep my family out of it." Then he's not corrupt. He's a hostage.
That changes the story. It doesn't kill it.
Midnight. Her rooftop. Fairy lights on a water tank, two plastic chairs, two cups of chai going cold.
Stay until sunrise.
Miss the first flight. Kabir Sir will kill you.
Catch the last flight back to camp.
Cricket first. She knows that.
Go. Before I ask you to stay.
You talk about everything except cricket. At 5 AM, Delhi turns pink. She falls asleep on your shoulder, still holding the red pen.
"I'm sorry. For all of it. Can we start again?"
Ask for a second chance.
Keep it professional.
Some chapters close.
Good luck in the camp, cricketer. I mean that.
...Slowly. Very slowly. Starting with you buying the chai.
Her phone buzzes. Her editor. She reads it twice, then turns the screen to you.
"Kill the Mehra story. Order from the top. The paper's owners sold thirty percent to Mehra Media last night."
He bought my newspaper. Overnight. To shut me up.
Raghav Mehra didn't threaten Neha. He just bought the ground she was standing on.
